[SLi-Rec (IJCAI 2019)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2019/0585.pdf) provides a direct adaptive-versus-fixed fusion comparison: Table 5 tests long-only, short-only, a tuned fixed mixture, and adaptive fusion. Adaptive fusion wins, but evaluation uses AUC rather than this benchmark’s HR@10. [CLSR (WWW 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13090) adds separate interest encoders, contrastive supervision, and adaptive aggregation. [Dual Stream Adaptive Sequential Recommendation](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-02282-0) compares fixed 50/50 fusion against a learned gate with identical dual-stream encoders, windows, and loss. These support the approach’s plausibility; none establishes the complete requested comparison against recent-only SASRec, recency pooling, and tuned fixed mixtures. Also, [SASRec itself](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) adaptively models both distant and recent interactions; “recent-only” describes a truncated variant.

Recommended controls, rather than established findings: compare full-history SASRec with several recent-window lengths; add exponential recency-weighted pooling; compare identical branches using validation-tuned fixed weights, a learned global scalar, and a context-dependent gate. Match parameter counts and GPU budgets with a larger single encoder or two-encoder fixed ensemble. Preserve identical positional indices when masking versus truncating histories, then separately test position resetting. Normalize each branch before fusion and report branch norms, gate distributions, and effective weighted contributions; otherwise gating may merely compensate for scale. Shuffle gate contexts across users to test whether contextual assignment matters. Require improvements in the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10, report category results and GPU seconds, and treat speculative upside as unproven until these cheaper controls are beaten.
